factual_methodological.summary: Bank of Israel July 2026 macro baselines, Ministry of Defense 2025 export record, CBS material and Energy Ministry gas-system claims were checked against primary institutional sources current to October 2026.

editorial_publication_readiness.summary: Israel and the occupied Palestinian territory are kept distinct as legal, statistical and analytical units; observed facts, mechanisms and conditional scenarios are separated.

novelty_against_existing_country_layer.summary: No canonical Israel country-context dossier exists; the report adds reusable context on institutions, high technology, defence, energy, demography, mobilisation and regional/Palestinian transmission.

visual_evidence_readiness.summary: Both locales contain one table, three charts, one flow, one mindmap and one functional geographic map. The map encodes transmission channels rather than borders, sovereignty claims or military routes.

political_neutrality.summary: Institutions, coalitions, conflicts and policy choices are described analytically without partisan or electoral endorsement.

contrary_evidence: High-technology exports, reserves and financial-system depth argue against a simple wartime-collapse thesis.
Security demand supports defence exports while imposing labour, fiscal and infrastructure costs.
Natural-gas exports create regional interdependence but do not remove infrastructure and geopolitical vulnerability.
limitations: Conflict-related fiscal and labour data are revision-prone and are explicitly dated.
Israeli official statistics, Palestinian statistics and data for occupied territories are not interchangeable.
Scenarios are conditional analytical paths rather than forecasts.
notes: Approved after primary-source verification current to 4 October 2026, bilingual parity review, controlled-taxonomy review, conflict-methodology review and addition of a functional geographic map.

en.title: Israel: security-state capacity, technological concentration and the fiscal-demographic limits of resilience
en.deck: Israel combines globally competitive technology and defence systems with unusually deep mobilisation capacity, but the post-2023 security burden, infrastructure gaps and uneven demographic participation increasingly determine whether resilience can remain fiscally and socially durable.
en.regime: High-capacity security state with globally competitive technology and finance, operating under a structurally higher post-2023 defence burden and demographic-infrastructure constraints that increasingly determine potential growth.
en.key_risk: Repeated regional mobilisation, rising debt and relocation of high-value technology functions could gradually erode the civilian tax base and productive infrastructure that finance Israel's security capacity.

pt-BR.title: Israel: capacidade de Estado de segurança, concentração tecnológica e limites fiscais e demográficos da resiliência
pt-BR.deck: Israel combina sistemas tecnológicos e de defesa globalmente competitivos com capacidade incomum de mobilização, mas o encargo de segurança pós-2023, gargalos de infraestrutura e participação demográfica desigual determinam cada vez mais a sustentabilidade fiscal e social da resiliência.
pt-BR.regime: Estado de segurança de alta capacidade, com tecnologia e finanças globalmente competitivas, operando sob encargo de defesa estruturalmente maior após 2023 e restrições demográficas e de infraestrutura que determinam cada vez mais o crescimento potencial.

publication.selection_rationale: The public corpus contains a focused study of Israel's 1985 stabilization but lacks a reusable country-level dossier linking state formation, constitutional institutions, security mobilisation, high technology, defence industry, fiscal capacity, demographics, energy and water systems, regional normalisation, and the economic mechanisms connecting Israel with the West Bank and Gaza. Israel is also directly connected to existing Iran, Saudi Arabia and United States country research, making a structural dossier necessary to avoid repeatedly rebuilding context in regional research.
contrary_evidence: Large foreign-exchange reserves, a resilient financial system, strong high-tech exports and repeated post-shock recoveries argue against a simple thesis of economic fragility.
Rising debt, repeated reserve mobilisation, infrastructure gaps and relocation of some R&D activity abroad argue against treating wartime resilience as costless or indefinitely self-renewing.

Peace treaties and regional normalisation demonstrate substantial interstate integration, while the unresolved Israeli-Palestinian conflict and continuing regional military confrontation limit any claim that geopolitical risk has structurally disappeared.
A young population can enlarge future labour supply, but uneven employment and skill formation across rapidly growing groups mean demographic growth is not automatically a fiscal dividend.
limitations: Israeli and Palestinian statistical systems use different territorial coverage; population and GDP series must not be combined without explicit scope reconciliation.
Wartime fiscal and defence figures use different accounting perimeters and are frequently revised as operations and reserves change.
Active-conflict casualty, damage and displacement figures can be incomplete or differently defined across Israeli, Palestinian and UN sources.
The ICJ source is an advisory opinion with separate and dissenting opinions; its legal conclusions are attributed precisely and not treated as a negotiated political settlement.
Current macroeconomic forecasts are highly conditional on security assumptions and differ between the IMF and Bank of Israel.
The 27 October 2026 election had not occurred by the evidence cutoff, so no electoral outcome is inferred.
